sections.title: How PRIMER dates a fire
sections.lead: PRIMER dates a hectare on the first day its accumulated fire probability inside a window of 14 days or less reaches 90%.
paragraphs: Probability is re-scored every 6 hours. A dated fire can drift after the call; below 80% it drops back to the watchlist.

PRIMER is the only model that measures fuel on the ground and puts a date on a fire. Live and dead fuel moisture sensors in every covered area feed it; the cat models and danger ratings below work from weather records, static fuel maps or modelled moisture.

sections.title: Lead time and window
paragraphs: Lead time is the number of days from the call to the first day of the window. The window is the span in which the hectare’s accumulated probability reaches the threshold; it starts wide and narrows as each issue is re-scored.
Example: PH-01 was called on 29 Sep, 15 days ahead, for 14–18 Oct; its window narrowed from 14 to 5 days.

sections.title: The Texas note
paragraphs: A month ahead in a monotonic dry season, narrowing to days inside the weather horizon. Texas has two seasons, and intermittent rain resets the fast clock.

terms.text: Burns in at least 90% of ensemble runs: the core of the fire. Its loss is the lower figure.
The expected footprint. Its loss is the point figure.
The tail if nothing intervenes. Its loss is the upper figure.
The spread between the P90 and P25 losses; the ELT’s SD is (upper − lower) ÷ 2.56.

sections.title: Mean damage ratio
paragraphs: Loss divided by replacement value, by fuel and construction: Frame 0.72, Masonry 0.55, Steel 0.45; utilities 0.15–0.35 by asset; rangeland about 0.30 across pasture, fencing and livestock.

sections.title: Ground-up and gross
paragraphs: Ground-up is the loss before policy terms. Gross applies a 2% deductible and a $1.2M per-location limit.

terms.text: Average annual loss: the long-run expected loss per year, often quoted per $1,000 of TIV. It is what the cat models produce and what rates were filed on.
Σ probability × point loss over the fires dated for the next 30 days. The alert card sums only the fires visible at the slider’s position.

sections.title: EP curve, OEP, return period and TVaR

terms.text: Exceedance probability: the chance in a year that a single event’s loss exceeds each amount.
The occurrence losses exceeded once in 100 and once in 250 years.
Where a loss sits on the book’s EP curve, stated as “a 1-in-N event for this book”.
Tail value at risk: the expected loss given that the return-period loss is exceeded.

sections.title: Technical premium and rate adequacy
paragraphs: The premium that pays PRIMER’s dated expected loss and its adjustment cost, covers the fixed and variable expenses and earns the target return: FE is $95 a policy, ALAE 12% of loss, VE 24% and RoP 6% of premium. Divided by TIV it is the PRIMER technical rate; rate adequacy is the market rate against it.

sections.title: Fuel moisture, ERC and timelag classes

terms.text: Water in living plants as a share of dry weight. Below about 80% the live fuel carries fire; with curing it sets the window (the slow clock).
1-h, 10-h, 100-h and 1000-h fuels: twigs to logs, named for how fast they follow the air’s humidity. The fine classes and the wind set the day (the fast clock).
The share of the grass that is dead. Above about 80% cured, grass fires run.
Energy release component: the heat available at the flaming front, read against the Texas 90th percentile.
Keetch–Byram drought index: 0 is saturated soil, 800 is absolute drought.

sections.title: Who pays for the plan
paragraphs: Fuel work on private land is the landowner plus a state cost-share (TPWD, TFS, NRCS EQIP). Corridor work and PSPS are the utility’s, rate-recoverable under an HB 145 wildfire plan. Structure defence and hardening are carrier-funded. A state agency plan is the state’s.
Across this book’s plans: 65% utilities, the state and counties; 18% landowners and operators; 17% the carrier.

sections.title: The scope rule
paragraphs: When the P50 footprint exceeds 2,000 ha or the plan would cost more than 40% of the loss it avoids, the plan narrows to homes ranked by TIV × damage ratio until the ratio holds. The map shows protected homes with a green ring and warned homes with an amber ring.

sections.title: What the loss includes, and what is not modelled
paragraphs: Every fire’s loss includes demand surge 18%, debris removal 5%, ALE and excludes smoke and urban conflagration beyond the band.
Not modelled: home-to-home urban conflagration and ember loss inside dense subdivisions, and smoke. ALE and demand surge are shown as inclusions on each fire, not inside the point loss.

terms.text: Total insured value: the rebuild value of the covered homes and assets.
The TIV and the count of locations inside a fire’s footprint.
The live-event convention: the P90, P50 and P25 losses.
The top 10 areas by exposed TIV, ring analysis around a fire, and linear accumulations along lines and pipelines.
Event loss table: event ID, rate (probability), mean loss, SD and exposure impacted.
The historical fire closest to this one in fuel, weather and terrain.
What the loss figure carries (demand surge, debris removal, ALE) and what it leaves out.
The share of locations geocoded to the building, and the flag on homes insured below their rebuild cost.
Loss ÷ premium; and the loss ratio plus the expense ratio.
What the carrier can credit after the work: a Class A roof, a 5 ft ember zone, an IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home.
The mean squared error of probability forecasts (lower is better), and whether events called at 90% happen 90% of the time.

terms.term: Non-renewal rate and FAIR Plan share
terms.text: Policies the market declined to renew, and the insurer of last resort’s share of the market.
